# Probability, and how a machine learns it {#sec-ch02}

Many people think probability is only about coins and dice, something from school maths that has nothing to do with building AI. This is a costly mistake. In this chapter we learn to read a probability correctly, see a common trap that even doctors fall into, and see how a machine learns probabilities from examples.

::: {.goals}
- Understand what "70% chance" really means, in a way you can check.
- Avoid the base-rate trap, and update a probability when new evidence comes.
- See how a machine learns a probability, and two ways it can fool you.
:::

## What "70% chance" means

Suppose the weather app says there is a 70% chance of rain tomorrow, and it does not rain. Was the app wrong?

One day cannot tell us. We need to look at many days. Take all the days when the app said "70%". If it rained on about 70 out of every 100 such days, the app is doing its job. Tomorrow was simply one of the other 30 days.

::: {.keyidea}
**A probability is a promise about many cases.** "70% chance of rain" means it rains on about 70 out of 100 such days. One dry day does not prove it wrong.
:::

This is useful because we can check it. When a model says "this alert is 70% likely to be an attack", it is making the same kind of promise as the weather app, and we can check it in the same way.

## The trap that fools doctors

Try this question before reading further. Suppose a test catches 99% of real attacks, but also raises a false alarm on 5% of normal activity, and real attacks are rare: about 1 in every 1,000 events. If the test raises an alarm, what is the chance that it is a real attack?

Most people answer about 95%. The correct answer is about **2%**. In a famous study from 1978, doctors at a top American medical college were asked the same question about a medical test, and the most common answer was also 95% [@casscells1978].

![The same puzzle, counted out. Of 100,000 events, 100 are attacks and the detector catches 99 of them. But 5% of the 99,900 normal events also set it off: 4,995 false alarms. When the alarm sounds, you're holding one of 5,094 alerts, and only 99 of them are real.](/figures/ch02/base-rate-tree.pdf){#fig-base-rate-tree}

The easy way to see this is to count, as in @fig-base-rate-tree. Take 100,000 events (one lakh). Only 100 are attacks, and the test catches 99 of them. But 5% of the 99,900 normal events also raise an alarm, which is 4,995 false alarms. So out of 5,094 alarms, only 99 are real. That is about 2%.

The chance before we see any evidence, here 1 in 1,000, is called the **base rate**. Forgetting the base rate is one of the most common mistakes with probability. This is why a fraud model that is "95% accurate" can still send a bank lakhs of false alarms. Whenever a probability surprises you, convert it into counts like this [@gigerenzer1995].

::: {.keyidea}
**First ask: how common is it to begin with?** If only 1 in 1,000 events is an attack, even a 99%-accurate alarm is right only about 2% of the time. Counting the cases makes this clear.
:::

There is a related mistake. "How often do attacks have a bad score?" and "How often is an alert with a bad score an attack?" are two different questions. In our example, only {{< num ch02 ioc_attack_share pct >}} of attacks come with a bad threat score, but an alert with a bad score is an attack {{< num ch02 p1 pct >}} of the time.

## Updating with new evidence

How should a new clue change our belief? It is easiest with **odds**. A probability of 20% means odds of 20 to 80, or 0.25. Each clue has a strength called the **likelihood ratio**: how many times more common the clue is among attacks than among harmless alerts. In our example, a bad threat score is about {{< num ch02 lr_ioc f1 >}} times more common among attacks.

New odds = old odds × strength of the clue. This is Bayes' rule.

![Starting from the base rate and multiplying the odds by each clue's likelihood ratio. Three ordinary clues take an alert from "probably nothing" to "probably an attack".](/figures/ch02/odds-update.pdf){#fig-odds-update}

An ordinary alert starts at {{< num ch02 base pct >}}. With a bad threat score, it goes up to {{< num ch02 p1 pct >}}. If it also happened outside office hours, it becomes {{< num ch02 p2 pct >}}. If the login was also from a new country, it becomes {{< num ch02 p3 pct >}} (@fig-odds-update). One caution: this assumes each clue gives new information. In real life, clues often overlap, so in practice we let a model learn how much each clue is worth.

## Why accuracy can mislead

Suppose our rule is: *mark an alert as an attack if its threat score is 0.5 or more.* Three common measures:

- **Precision**: when the rule raises an alarm, how often is it a real attack? Here, {{< num ch02 precision pct >}}.
- **Recall**: out of all real attacks, how many does the rule catch? Here, {{< num ch02 recall pct >}}.
- **Accuracy**: out of all alerts, how many did the rule judge correctly? Here, {{< num ch02 accuracy pct >}}.

![Every one of the 20,000 alerts, sorted by what the rule said and what really happened. Precision and recall each ignore one of the two columns, which makes them fair judges of rare events.](/figures/ch02/confusion.pdf){#fig-confusion}

The accuracy of {{< num ch02 accuracy pct >}} sounds good. But a rule that *never* raises any alarm has an accuracy of {{< num ch02 always_benign_acc pct >}}. When one outcome is rare, accuracy mostly measures how common the other outcome is. So for rare events, look at precision and recall.

## How a machine learns a probability

Bayes' rule multiplies odds. Adding is easier than multiplying, so we take the logarithm of the odds, and then each clue simply adds a number. This gives a very simple model: start with a base number, add a **weight** for each clue, and convert the total into a probability using an S-shaped curve. This model is called **logistic regression**. Banks and hospitals have used it for decades for credit scores and risk scores.

![The S-curve (the logistic, or sigmoid, function) turns total evidence into a probability. Every step to the right multiplies the odds by the same amount, which is why the curve flattens out: once you're very sure, more evidence changes the probability only a little.](/figures/ch03/sigmoid.pdf){#fig-sigmoid}

To find good weights, we need a way to score a probability. If the model says 90% and the event happens, it should lose very few points. If it says 1% and the event happens, it should lose many points, because it was confident and wrong. This score is called **log loss**.

![Log loss for a single alert. If it really was an attack (red, solid curve), the penalty is small when the model gave "attack" a high probability. It grows very fast as that probability gets close to zero. Harmless alerts (blue, dashed curve) work the same way from the other side.](/figures/ch03/logloss.pdf){#fig-logloss}

Log loss has an important property. The only way to get the best score, on average, is to give honest probabilities (@fig-logloss). If a model exaggerates and says 99% when the truth is 80%, it loses more over many cases. So models trained with log loss tend to give honest probabilities.

Training means finding the weights with the lowest log loss. Imagine standing on a hill in thick fog. You cannot see the bottom, but you can feel which way the ground slopes. So you take a small step downhill, and repeat. This method is called **gradient descent**.

::: {.keyidea}
**All machine learning is one loop.** Predict, measure the mistake, adjust a little, and repeat. From logistic regression to ChatGPT, only the size of the model changes.
:::
## Two ways a model fools you

**Overfitting** means memorising instead of learning. A very flexible model can remember every small detail of its training data, including random noise. It then looks excellent on that data but performs badly on new cases. @fig-overfit shows this with a decision tree, a model that sorts cases by asking a series of yes/no questions: the more questions it may ask, the more it memorises. The only way to catch this is to test the model on data it has never seen.

![A decision tree allowed only a few questions learns general patterns. Allowed dozens, it memorises individual training alerts: its loss on them approaches zero while its loss on new alerts climbs.](/figures/ch03/overfit.pdf){#fig-overfit}

**Leakage** means a clue secretly contains the answer. For example, if we train with the analysts' notes, results look amazing, because notes like "confirmed phishing" are written *after* someone has already decided. When the model has to decide, that note does not exist yet. So for every clue, ask: *will I really have this information at the moment of the decision?*

::: {.exercises}
1. A spam filter catches 98% of spam and wrongly flags 1% of normal emails. If only 1% of all emails are spam, what fraction of flagged emails are actually normal? Use counts, as in @fig-base-rate-tree.
:::
